results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All eleven outline summaries match the controlling ideas of p01 to p11 in order; the p10 summary omits the Waypoint decisions and the order callback but keeps the core (unowned facts at the handoffs, owner before product).

Introduction ¶2 (p02), marked two_ideas by the outliner, holds one idea: the scope sentence (business before technology) is drawn from the claim as its consequence, as the spec's idea declares. The 'therefore' is thin (flow reader 2) but the paragraph is not double.

results.quote: [[commerce-business-models]] explains **how the buyer and sales channel change the system requirements**. [...] The chapter names four such business shapes, from Starting to Group, as scale stages: a merchant moves from one to the next by adding channels, locations and brands, not by passing a revenue figure.
results.finding: The spec's single idea is that the shape of the business decides the systems, with the scale stages as its named cases; the draft never states that idea, so the paragraph reads as two: buyer and channel change the requirements, and, separately, four scale stages exist. The outliner and both flow readers read it as two things.
p01 to p04, p10 and p11 trace to the part's claim; p05 to p09 each introduce the chapter arguing P1-1 to P1-5 in turn.

Every evidence item is followed by words on what it shows (e.g. 'shows the normal path', 'exposes missing capabilities and overlapping writers', 'test whether a new product would solve'), and the three captions each say what the figure shows.

All declared transitions are readable at their boundaries ('From that order', 'tests that claim on one example', 'examines that company with five questions', 'The steps of the journey stay the same, but', 'then maps', 'The map says ... but it cannot settle', 'comes last, once', 'Together, the five answers'), and the hand-off names journey-of-an-order as the concrete case of the claim. Note: p11's cause is carried by its second sentence ('because each answer builds on the one before'), not its first.

Both flow readers describe a narrowing opening (order, claim, company, questions), a chapter list in the announced prerequisite order and a closing sum, which agrees with large_to_small and prerequisite_order; no section's position is unclear and neither wants anything moved. Single-reader, sentence-level re-reads not failed: KEY POINTS bullet 3 is dense (both readers re-read it, neither lost the thread); 'order' as sequence; 'the number' before stock is named; the three-status clause in p05; thirteen systems and thirteen steps.

results.quote: The chapter names four such business shapes, from Starting to Group, as scale stages: a merchant moves from one to the next by adding channels, locations and brands, not by passing a revenue figure.
results.finding: Flow reader 1: "'four such' seemed to mean those [four buyers]. 'Starting to Group' is a different, unexplained axis. This was the one real break." The order is sound; the prose makes 'four such business shapes' point back at the four buyers when it means stages of the business, and no sentence says how the two relate.
results.corroborated_by: flow reader 2, section 3, item 1 (Lost the thread)

results.finding: Every term on does_not_know is glossed in a clause where it first appears: shop platform, writers, capabilities, record and copy, scale stages, Eva; Waypoint and Noor Visser are re-introduced. Minor, one reader only: 'shop' is used once for a wholesale buyer where it otherwise means the webshop (flow reader 1).
Opens on a concrete order and states a disputable claim in the second paragraph; none of the five weak patterns.
The closing synthesizes and gives a course of action; no new subtopic, no bare restatement, no body evidence beyond the one-clause reference to Kestrel & Pine's unowned facts.

p10 states the five answers as one line of reasoning leading to the 2027 Waypoint decisions, names unowned facts at the handoffs that no replacement product would fix, and ends on the so-what: look at the handoffs and ask who owns the fact before asking which product to buy.
'The shopper's one order shows the same thing once it is followed past the storefront' returns to p01's order, and p11 sends the reader to the chapter that follows it.
The intro-only reader predicted the five chapters, one per question, in the roadmap's order, with Kestrel & Pine as the running example and a possible hand-off to the first chapter.
The cold reader named the five subjects in order: order journey, business models, capability map, systems of record, platform landscape.

The cold reader chose boundaries-and-systems-of-record for (a), citing the authoritative owner and records against copies, and commerce-platform-landscape for (b), citing the categories, operating costs and the two rebuild proposals.

The cold reader gave all three expected reasons: the journey is the concrete case and supplies the steps later chapters build on, each answer is the next question's vocabulary, and products can be judged only once jobs are mapped and owners named.
